title: MonoScale: Scaling Multi-Agent System with Monotonic Improvement
claim: Naively adding more components to a system without adaptation yields non-monotonic, often degraded performance, so scaling up is unstable.
layout: single grouped bar chart, left-to-right, value labels above bars
description: A grouped bar chart on a white background with dashed horizontal gridlines. The y-axis is labeled GAIA score and runs from 0.40 to 0.70. A legend at top left lists four agent pool sizes (3, 5, 7 and 10 Agents) in progressively darker slate-gray shades. Each cluster of four bars appears to be one router model, and every bar has its exact value printed above it. In the first cluster the values are 0.448, 0.436, 0.461 and 0.424. In the second they are 0.515, 0.558, 0.545 and 0.491. In the third they are 0.606, 0.655, 0.527 and a partly visible fourth bar. The scores rise and then fall as the pool grows, and the 10-agent bar is consistently low. The eye goes first to the uneven bar heights. The crop cuts off the right side and the bottom, including the x-axis labels.
caption: Motivation for MonoScale: without an expansion-aware familiarization and update mechanism, routers cold-start on newly added agents, causing unstable routing decisions and potential performance collapse during scale-up. Bars show GAIA scores for different agent pool sizes (N ∈{3, 5, 7, 10}) under cold-start routers (Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-V3.2, and Gemini-3-Pro).
abstract: In recent years, LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have advanced rapidly, using a router to decompose tasks and delegate subtasks to specialized agents. A natural way to expand capability is to scale up the agent pool by continually integrating new functional agents or tool interfaces, but naive expansion can trigger performance collapse when the router cold-starts on newly added, heterogeneous, and unreliable agents. We propose MonoScale, an expansion-aware update framework that proactively generates a small set of agent-conditioned familiarization tasks, harvests evidence from both successful and failed interactions, and distills it into auditable natural-language memory to guide future routing. We formalize sequential augmentation as a contextual bandit and perform trust-region memory updates, yielding a monotonic non-decreasing performance guarantee across onboarding rounds. Experiments on GAIA and Humanity's Last Exam show stable gains as the agent pool grows, outperforming naive scale-up and strong-router fixed-pool baselines.
